invitation: A prophet on a mountain, a soldier in a pub, a bishop at breakfast and a child in a schoolyard, across a little under a century. Three read here in the page and the whole drop is quick.

pieces.title: On the Pitiful (from Thus Spoke Zarathustra)
pieces.author: Friedrich Nietzsche (translated by Thomas Common)
pieces.note: A page of aphorisms in a prophet's voice. Notice how short each sentence is, how the speaker keeps swinging between 'I' and 'you', and how often a bold claim is followed at once by a small concrete instruction. Look for the places where he answers an objection before the reader has raised it.

pieces.title: Gunga Din
pieces.author: Rudyard Kipling
pieces.note: A ballad in a Victorian soldier's dialect, built to be spoken aloud. Notice how the shouted refrain changes meaning each time it returns, how the spelling does the work of characterisation, and what the speaker is only able to say in the last line. Be warned that the voice and vocabulary are those of a colonial soldier, and ask whose speech the poem lets you hear and whose it does not.

pieces.title: The Bishop's Candlesticks (extract from Les Misérables)
pieces.author: Victor Hugo (translated by Isabel F. Hapgood)
pieces.note: A self-contained scene from the novel, readable on its own. Notice how casual the Bishop's speech is, how brisk and procedural the gendarmes are by contrast, and how little he explains to the man he is speaking to. Look at the final paragraph and what the narrator admits he cannot tell you.

pieces.title: Coat of Many Colors
pieces.author: Dolly Parton
pieces.note: A lyric that tells a single childhood incident in plain chronological order. Notice how specific the details of the sewing are, how the schoolyard scene is given in very few words, and how the last verse changes what the earlier ones were for. Listen to how modest the tune is, and how the story is left to carry the song.
